FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Nature Club Animals flashcards.

Twenty-two spotter sheets for children who already know their animal families and want to go deeper — this is the Nature Club deck, the step up from Animal Categories. Each card studies one specialist group: the hunters of the sky, the shells of the shore, the animals that pollinate our food, the whole dog family from wolf to dingo, and the wild homes from grassland to mountaintop. Each card page carries a simple guide a kid can follow, and every card opens its own Nature Club lesson on its own page.

THE CARDS

Every card in the set.

Each card has its own page, and every card shows its age pill — start with the group that fits your child today.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    The Spotter's Walk

    Take one card on your walk — birds-of-prey on the park day, garden-birds any day — and count what you actually spot from its squares. Real animals are everywhere once you have a card in your pocket.

  2. 02

    The deeper deck

    This set steps up from Animal Categories: same two-by-two sheets, closer study. Read one square a day and ask "how is this animal different from its cousin beside it?" A hawk and a falcon look alike — until they don’t.

  3. 03

    Same animal, two names

    The cards carry the ocean-crossing names: the reindeer of Lapland is the caribou of Canada, a prawn in Britain is a shrimp in America, and a buzzard means two different birds on two sides of the Atlantic. Both names are right.

  4. 04

    Family tree game

    Lay the dog-family card beside the pets card: which animals are cousins? Then rodents beside small-animals, garden-birds beside birds. The deeper deck keeps meeting the first deck — cousins everywhere.

  5. 05

    Draw the one you met

    After a spotting walk, draw the real creature you saw next to the card version. A notebook of met animals is the Nature Club badge of honor — one page per walk, no rush.

      Birds of Prey Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Birds of the world

      Birds of prey are the hunters of the sky: hooked beaks, sharp talons and eyes that can spot a rabbit from higher than a rooftop. On the card, four famous hunters perch in their squares — the eagle, the hawk, the falcon and the fish-loving osprey.

      Say it together

      “Birds of prey! They hunt with their eyes and their feet. The eagle is the giant, the hawk circles round and round, the falcon is the fastest animal on Earth when it dives, and the osprey catches fish straight out of the water — splash!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hawk eyes minute: sit by a window and find three tiny things a hawk might spot from the sky — a coin, a leaf, a crack in the path. Sharp eyes are the hunting tool; practice is the game.

      Quick parent note

      Birds of prey are also called raptors, from a Latin word that means to seize and carry away. A peregrine falcon’s dive tops 300 kilometers an hour — faster than any other animal, ever.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Birds of Prey lesson on the Learning Path.

      Garden Birds Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 3+Birds of the world

      The backyard is a bird neighborhood, and this card holds four familiar neighbors: the robin with its bright chest, the woodpecker that drums on trees, the blue jay in its sharp blue suit, and the cardinal in its all-red coat. On the card, the feeder’s regulars sit in their squares.

      Say it together

      “Garden birds! The robin hops close to see who you are, the woodpecker taps the tree — tok-tok-tok — the blue jay squawks the news, and the cardinal is the reddest bird in the yard. Who is visiting YOUR feeder today?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Counting feeder: fill a simple feeder (or scatter seeds) and keep a tally with stickers — one per bird visit. Which card bird shows up most? Real bird counts like this help real scientists, too.

      Quick parent note

      Woodpeckers drum up to 20 times a second and have a built-in helmet for the pounding. The cardinal and the blue jay are famous in US and Canadian yards; the robin in Britain is the little red-breasted bird that follows gardeners around.

      Teach it, step by step

      Desert Birds Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Birds of the world

      Birds live even in the hottest desert, and each one has a trick: the roadrunner that sprints instead of flying, the desert owl that sleeps the day away, the vulture that soars for hours without flapping, and the sandgrouse that carries water to its chicks in its feathers. On the card, four desert specialists wait in their squares.

      Say it together

      “Desert birds! The roadrunner runs — beep beep! — faster than most birds fly, the desert owl naps in the shade all day, the vulture rides the warm wind round and round, and the sandgrouse flies far to bring water home in its belly feathers!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Roadrunner relay: race across the yard on foot — running style only, wings optional. Then float around the room with still arms like a vulture riding the hot wind, without a single flap.

      Quick parent note

      This card carries a famous word mix-up: in North America a buzzard is a vulture like the one on this card, but in Britain a buzzard is a hawk — same word, two birds. Sandgrouse fathers truly soak their belly feathers and fly up to 30 kilometers for water.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Desert Birds lesson on the Learning Path.

      Australian Birds Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Birds of the world

      Australia’s birds are unlike anywhere else on Earth: the emu, a giant flightless runner; the kookaburra whose call sounds like laughter; the cassowary with its helmet and dagger claw; and the lyrebird, the world’s best copycat, which can mimic almost any sound it hears. On the card, the Australian four hold their squares.

      Say it together

      “Australian birds! The emu is taller than a grown-up and runs instead of flying, the kookaburra laughs at the sky — ha-ha-ha — the cassowary wears a hard helmet, and the lyrebird can copy car alarms, chainsaws and other birds, perfectly!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Kookaburra song: learn the old song "Kookaburra sits in the old gum tree" and try your best laugh-call. Then play copycat like the lyrebird: repeat every sound the leader makes for one whole minute.

      Quick parent note

      The emu and cassowary are ratites — giant birds that gave up flying for running, like the ostrich. The lyrebird’s mimicry is real and astonishing: courtship is a full sound concert of borrowed voices.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Australian Birds lesson on the Learning Path.

      Coastal Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 3+By the water

      Where the land meets the sea, life gets lively: the seal that naps on warm rocks, the sea lion that can walk on its flippers and bark like a dog, the pelican with a pouch under its beak big enough for a whole lunch, and the puffin, the little sea parrot with the painted beak. On the card, the shore crew sits in its squares.

      Say it together

      “Coastal animals! The seal slides on its belly, the sea lion claps and barks, the pelican scoops fish in its pouch — scoop! — and the puffin flies underwater with its wings. The beach is their kitchen!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Beach moves: wriggle like a seal on a rug, walk on all fours and bark like a sea lion, stretch your arms into a pouch and scoop a "fish" from the blue carpet, then flap-splash like a puffin.

      Quick parent note

      Seals and sea lions are cousins with an easy tell: sea lions have little ear flaps and can rotate their back flippers to walk; true seals scoot on their bellies. A puffin’s beak lights up in rainbow colors only for breeding season.

      Teach it, step by step

      River Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 3+By the water

      A river is a moving road with its own crew: the otter that slides down the mudbank for fun, the beaver that builds dams and lodges with its teeth, the pink river dolphin that swims through flooded forests, and the crocodile sunning on the bank. On the card, the river four drift through their squares.

      Say it together

      “River animals! The otter plays and slides all day, the beaver builds a house of sticks — slap goes its tail! The river dolphin swims in the big slow rivers, and the crocodile floats like a log with eyes. Careful stepping, crocodile territory!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Otter slide: socks on a smooth floor, run and slide — otters slide for fun, that is the whole lesson. Then build a "dam" of cushions that actually holds back a wave of rolled socks.

      Quick parent note

      Otters are among the few animals that play with no purpose at all — sliding is real. River dolphins are born grey and turn pink with age and sun. An alligator vs crocodile tell: alligators have wide U-snouts and like fresh water; crocodiles have pointy V-snouts and can live in the sea.

      Teach it, step by step

      Wetland Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5By the water

      The wetland is the swampy meeting place of land and water, and it runs on patient legs: the heron that stands so still fish forget it is there, the stork with its long legs and bigger stories, the alligator ruling the warm marshes, and the muskrat paddling its round tail through the reeds. On the card, the marsh crew wades through its squares.

      Say it together

      “Wetland animals! The heron stands like a statue — one fish, please! The stork struts on stilts, the alligator glides with just its eyes above the water, and the muskrat paddles its own little boat of a body. Shhh — the marsh is listening.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Heron statue game: freeze like a hunting heron for ten whole seconds, then snap your neck forward to catch a sock-fish. The stillness is the skill — and it is harder than it sounds.

      Quick parent note

      Wetlands are the world’s sponges: they soak up floods and clean the water on the way through. Herons sometimes hunt with bait — dropping a crumb or feather on the water and catching the fish that come to look. Fishing with tools, with feathers.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Wetland Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      Crustaceans Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5By the water

      Crustaceans are the armored swimmers and clingers: joints, shells and way too many legs to count quickly. On the card, four shell-backed characters hold their squares — the lobster with two different claws, the shrimp that swims backwards, the crayfish that is basically a freshwater lobster, and the barnacle that glues itself to rocks head-first and eats with its feet.

      Say it together

      “Crustaceans! Shells on the outside, legs everywhere. The lobster has a big crusher claw and a small snipper claw, the shrimp snaps backwards to escape, the crayfish hides under river rocks, and the barnacle stands on its head in one spot forever!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Crab-walk tag: scuttle sideways, and when tagged, freeze in a shrimp-tail curl. Count the legs on a toy crab or shrimp — ten walking legs, plus claws. Too many legs is the family trademark.

      Quick parent note

      The word pair rides on this card: Americans say shrimp, the British say prawn — same little swimmer, either name. A lobster’s two claws do different jobs, and it can take five to seven years to grow big enough to be legal to catch.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Crustaceans lesson on the Learning Path.

      Shellfish Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5By the water

      Some sea animals carry their whole house on their body: the clam buried in the sand, the mussel glued in rows to the rocks, the oyster that can grow a pearl inside its shell, and the nautilus, a living fossil that steers its spiral shell up and down the deep water like a submarine. On the card, four shelled wonders sit in their squares.

      Say it together

      “Shellfish! Animals with shells instead of bones. The clam hides in the sand and spits little fountains, the mussels hold hands with threads to stay on the rocks, the oyster makes pearls from sand it did not want, and the nautilus is a spiral shell with a tentacled pilot inside!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Shell sorting bowl: mix clean shells (or pasta shells) and sort by spiral, fan and flat. Open a real mussel shell and find the hinge — every shellfish shell has its own closing trick.

      Quick parent note

      Pearls happen when a grain of sand slips inside an oyster and the oyster wraps it in smooth, pearly layers — thousands of layers, over years. The nautilus has barely changed in 500 million years: the deep sea’s original submarine.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Shellfish lesson on the Learning Path.

      Deep-Sea Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5By the water

      Far below where sunlight reaches, the ocean has a midnight crew: the anglerfish that fishes with a glowing lure, the giant squid with eyes the size of dinner plates, the manta ray that flies through the water like a huge black kite, and the sea turtle that crosses whole oceans and comes home to the beach where it hatched. On the card, the deep crew glides through its squares.

      Say it together

      “Deep-sea animals! Down where the sun cannot reach, it is dark — so some animals make their own light! The anglerfish dangles a glowing fishing rod, the giant squid has the biggest eyes in the animal kingdom, the manta ray flaps like a giant bird, and the sea turtle swims across the whole ocean and finds its way home.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Glow-in-the-dark angler: tape a small battery tea-light to a rod or stick, dim the room, and fish for paper fish with paperclip mouths. The glow-in-the-dark trick is how real anglers hunt in the dark.

      Quick parent note

      The anglerfish’s lure glows with help from glowing bacteria — a built-in nightlight for hunting. Sea turtles return to nest on the very beach where they were born, navigating by Earth’s magnetic field like sailors with an invisible compass.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Deep-Sea Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      Pollinators Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 3+Little crawlies

      Pollinators carry pollen from flower to flower, and almost every apple, strawberry and tomato on the table started with one of them: the honeybee that dances to tell its hive where the flowers are, the bumblebee that buzzes in the cold, the hummingbird that hovers like a tiny helicopter, and the bat that pollinates the night flowers. On the card, the flower-friends hold their squares.

      Say it together

      “Pollinators! They visit flowers for a sweet drink and carry the yellow dust — pollen — to the next flower, and that is how fruit begins! The honeybee dances the directions, the bumblebee buzzes in the cold morning, the hummingbird sips while hovering, and the bat does the night shift.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pollination tag: tape paper "pollen dots" to your child’s fingers, and move them from flower cup to flower cup — every transfer makes a fruit sticker appear. Bees really do dance: watch a short video of the waggle dance together.

      Quick parent note

      One in every three bites of food exists because a pollinator carried pollen. The bat on this card is a repeat visitor from the night-animals idea — bats pollinate bananas, mangoes and agave. Bumblebees can fly in colder weather than honeybees: they are the early-season specialists.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pollinators lesson on the Learning Path.

      Invertebrates Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Little crawlies

      Most animals on Earth have no backbone at all, and this card holds four of the cleverest: the octopus with nine brains and three hearts, the earthworm recycling the soil, the snail carrying its spiral house, and the starfish that can regrow a lost arm. On the card, the backbonless wonders sit in their squares.

      Say it together

      “Invertebrates! Animals with no bones inside — some wear shells instead, and some are just squishy and strong. The octopus is the smartest animal without a spine, the earthworm makes the garden grow, the snail carries its house everywhere, and the starfish pulls itself along on hundreds of tiny feet.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      No-bones day: move across the room like each invertebrate — slither like a worm, glide slow like a snail, stretch five arms like a starfish, and curl your arms into eight "tentacles" like an octopus. Bones optional; imagination not.

      Quick parent note

      The octopus can change color and texture in under a second and unscrews jar lids in labs. Invertebrates are roughly 97 out of every 100 animal species on Earth — the backbone is the rare thing to have, not the common one.

      Teach it, step by step

      Spiders & Ticks Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Little crawlies

      The eight-legged crew is its own group — arachnids, not insects: the garden spider spinning its wheel web, the big hairy tarantula that is gentler than it looks, the tick that waits in the tall grass, and the harvestman, the long-legged "daddy longlegs" that is not a spider at all. On the card, the arachnids sit in their squares.

      Say it together

      “Spiders and ticks! Eight legs, two body parts, no antennae — arachnids! The spider spins silk from its own body, the tarantula wears fuzzy pants, the tick waits patiently in the grass, and the harvestman strolls by on stilt legs.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Web engineering: wind wool or string between chair legs into a web with at least three sizes of gap, then toss pom-pom "bugs" — which gap catches? Silk is stronger than steel of the same weight: say it out loud, then test it.

      Quick parent note

      The tick is the card’s safety lesson said kindly: after walks in tall grass or woods, do a quick tick check — and a grown-up removes any tick with steady fingers or fine tweezers. Harvestmen are not spiders: one body piece, no silk, no venom. Spiders almost never bother people — they are busy pest control.

      Teach it, step by step

      The Dog Family Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 3+Fur families

      Your family dog has wild cousins on every continent: the wolf that hunts in a pack with its family, the coyote that has learned to live near towns, the arctic fox dressed in winter white, and the dingo, Australia’s wild dog. On the card, the canine cousins stand in their squares.

      Say it together

      “The dog family! Wolves live in family packs and howl at the moon — arooooo! The coyote is clever and quick, the arctic fox grows a white coat for winter, and the dingo is the wild dog of Australia. Your puppy at home? Same big family, smallest member!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pack howl: the family howls together, one at a time then all at once — wolves howl to say "we are here, all together." Then walk a "patrol" around the yard like coyotes, staying exactly together.

      Quick parent note

      A wolf pack is a family: mother, father and the pups of past years, hunting together. The arctic fox survives nights of −50°C — the warmest coat in the family. Domestic dogs came from wolves, which makes the wolf the ancestor of every good boy.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the The Dog Family lesson on the Learning Path.

      Deer & Grazers Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Fur families

      The grass-eaters with hooves run this card: the moose, the tallest wild animal in the northern forests; the reindeer, the sled-puller of the far north; the bison, the great shaggy heavyweight of the American plains; and the antelope, the sprinter with the spring in its step. On the card, the grazers graze in their squares.

      Say it together

      “Deer and grazers! They eat grass and leaves all day and run fast. The moose is huge with a wide antler crown, the reindeer pulls sleds through the snow, the bison is a big brown wall of fur, and the antelope bounces like the grass is a trampoline!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Grazer lunch: try grazing like a real herbivore — a plate of spinach leaves, celery and carrots, eaten slowly, grazing-style. Then gallop in place like an antelope while a grown-up moose-calls: a low "muuuh" from the cupped hands.

      Quick parent note

      The ocean-crossing names ride on this card: the reindeer of Europe and Asia is the caribou of Canada and Alaska — same animal, two names; and the moose is called the elk in Britain. Only reindeer grow antlers in both sexes — even the girls pull the sled.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Deer & Grazers lesson on the Learning Path.

      Rodents Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Fur families

      Rodents are the gnawers: front teeth that never stop growing, so they never stop chewing — and the world is better kept for it. On the card, four famous gnawers hold their squares: the squirrel planning acorn banks, the porcupine wearing a quill coat, the chinchilla with the softest fur on Earth, and the prairie dog that builds whole underground towns.

      Say it together

      “Rodents! Their teeth grow and grow, so they gnaw and gnaw — that is the whole family trick! The squirrel buries acorns, the porcupine says "don’t touch" with its quills, the chinchilla is the softest animal you can name, and the prairie dog kisses its neighbors hello in the tunnel town!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tooth-truth demo: find what a pencil, an acorn and a cardboard box have in common — rodents can chew all three. Then build a "prairie dog town" of tunnels from cushions and take turns popping up with a hello kiss (air kiss, prairie-dog style).

      Quick parent note

      Rodents are the biggest family in the mammal world — about 4 in every 10 mammal species. A chinchilla’s fur is so dense that water cannot reach its skin: it cleans with dust baths instead. Porcupine quills are modified hairs with tiny barbs — impressive, and best admired from the front.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      African Grassland Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Wild homes

      The African savanna is the great grass stage, and this card holds four of its stars: the lion resting between hunts, the cheetah, the fastest sprinter on land, the wildebeest that migrates in herds of over a million, and the ostrich, the biggest bird alive — which runs instead of flying. On the card, the grassland cast stands in its squares.

      Say it together

      “African grassland animals! The lion naps in the shade — even kings need naps! The cheetah runs as fast as a car on the highway, the wildebeest walks in herds bigger than a whole town, and the ostrich is a bird that sprints — and lays the biggest egg on Earth!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Grassland sprint test: measure a straight course, run it three times like a cheetah, then try ostrich style — big strides, wings tucked. Then lie in the shade like a lion and count who is breathing hardest.

      Quick parent note

      A cheetah’s sprint lasts about 20 seconds — speed costs everything, so it rests between chases. The wildebeest migration is the biggest overland journey of any animal on Earth. The ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain, and its kick can discourage a lion.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the African Grassland Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      South American Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Wild homes

      South America holds its own cast of characters: the llama, the woolly carrier of the mountain trails; the sloth, the slow-motion treetop resident; the jaguar, the strongest bite in the big cats; and the capybara, the world’s largest rodent and the friendliest animal on any card. On the card, the South American four relax in their squares.

      Say it together

      “South American animals! The llama carries loads up the mountains, the sloth does everything in slow motion, the jaguar swims AND climbs, and the capybara — a guinea pig the size of a dog! — gets along with every animal in the river.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Capybara hot spring: fill a basin with warm water, and every toy in the house is invited — capybaras famously share their baths with anyone. Then a llama obstacle walk: carry a small backpack across a cushion trail without dropping it.

      Quick parent note

      Jaguars have the strongest bite of any big cat — they can crack a turtle shell — and they love water, unlike most cats. Capybaras are so calm that birds sit on their heads; they are basically giant guinea pigs with a hammock lifestyle.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      More Arctic Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Wild homes

      The Arctic deserves a second look, because its winter residents are specialists: the arctic hare that turns white for the snow, the snowy owl that hunts in broad daylight, the musk ox that looks like a walking haystack and smells like its name, and the arctic tern — the champion traveler of the whole animal kingdom, flying pole to pole every year. On the card, the deep-winter crew stands in its squares.

      Say it together

      “More arctic animals! The arctic hare wears a white coat in winter and brown in summer, the snowy owl hunts even when the sun never sets, the musk ox huddles in a circle with its family, and the arctic tern flies from the top of the world to the bottom and back — every single year!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Coat-change game: one side of the room is summer (brown scarf), the other winter (white scarf) — run and change coats as the caller switches seasons. Then a migration flight: cross the room twice without landing, like the tern does over whole oceans.

      Quick parent note

      The arctic tern’s yearly round trip is about 70,000 kilometers — the longest migration of any animal, ever. Arctic hares can sprint at 60 kilometers an hour across the snow. This card is the Nature Club’s second visit to the ice — the first was the arctic-animals card in Animal Categories.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      Cave Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Wild homes

      Caves are the darkest homes on Earth, and the animals that live there have made amazing trades: the cave bat that navigates by echoes, the pale salamander, the cave cricket that hops in the pitch black, and the olm — a blind, pearl-white amphibian that lives its whole hundred-year life in the dark. On the card, the cave crew waits in its squares.

      Say it together

      “Cave animals! No sunlight down here — ever! The bat flies by listening to echoes, the salamander has skin the color of the pale moon, the cave cricket hops without seeing, and the olm is white as a ghost, blind as a stone, and can live for a hundred years!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Echo location: one person closes their eyes and calls "where am I?", and the other answers from a new spot — the listener points. Bats "see" with sound exactly this way. Then draw what you think the olm looks like before checking the card.

      Quick parent note

      The olm is the cave’s legend: blind, white, almost never moves, and lives up to a century — scientists have counted individuals sitting in the same spot for over seven years. Cave crickets leave the cave at night to find food and carry it back like delivery workers.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      Mountain Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Wild homes

      The high mountains have thin air, cold wind and steep cliffs — and animals dressed for all three: the mountain goat that walks ledges no person would dare, the snow leopard with its long tail for balance, the yak that carries everything at high altitude, and the marmot that whistles to warn its neighbors. On the card, the climbers hold their squares.

      Say it together

      “Mountain animals! Up where the air is thin and the rocks are steep. The mountain goat climbs sheer cliffs like stairs, the snow leopard balances with its giant fluffy tail, the yak walks through snow like it is nothing, and the marmot whistles — tweet! — to say "eagle overhead!"”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Balance-beak mountain: walk a line of tape on the floor with arms up like a snow leopard’s tail — the balance is the trick. Then a marmot whistle drill: one person hides a toy and whistles twice; the finder locates it.

      Quick parent note

      Mountain goats have rubbery pads built into their hooves — nature’s climbing shoes. The snow leopard’s tail is as long as its body and works as both balance beam and scarf. Marmots sleep up to eight months a year: the world’s longest winter nap.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      More Mountain Animals Flashcard for Wildlife

      Ages 4–5Wild homes

      The mountains get a second card, because the high life is crowded: the ibex with its great curved horns, the chamois that leaps between rocks like elastic, the pika — the tiny cousin of rabbits that stacks hay for winter — and the condor, one of the biggest flying birds on Earth, riding the mountain wind for hours. On the card, the second climbing crew takes its squares.

      Say it together

      “More mountain animals! The ibex has horns curved like bananas, the chamois bounces from rock to rock — boing! — the pika squeaks from its haystack, and the condor flies with wings wider than a car without flapping once!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Haystack relay: like the pika, collect "hay" (balls of paper) from one side of the room and stack a winter pile on the other — against a timer. Then glide with still arms from wall to wall like a condor: no flapping allowed.

      Quick parent note

      The pika does not hibernate — it spends the summer cutting grass and drying it into haystacks for winter lunch. A condor can ride the wind for hours and cover hundreds of kilometers with almost no wingbeats. The ibex’s horns grow a ring every year: you can count its age.
